title: Sub-lemma 1: distributional identity Y =d X (independence across columns)

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
**Goal.** In the matrix coupling for rational $p=k_0/n_0$ (matrix $M$ is $n\times m$, $n=n_0t$, $k=k_0t$, each column has a single $1$ in a uniform row, rows $r_1,\dots,r_n$, $y_i=\langle w,r_i\rangle$, $S\subseteq[n]$ uniform of size $k$, $Y=\sum_{i\in S}y_i$), prove
$$Y \stackrel{d}{=} X=\langle w,v\rangle,\qquad v\sim\mathrm{Bern}(p)^m.$$

**What must be shown (not just marginals).** It suffices to prove $\sum_{i\in S}r_i \stackrel{d}{=} v$. The published sketch only checks that the $j$-th coordinate of $\sum_{i\in S}r_i$ equals $1$ with probability $|S|/n=k/n=p$. A rigorous proof must additionally establish:
1. **Independence across columns.** Columns of $M$ are filled independently, so for any fixed $S$ and any $T\subseteq[m]$, $\Pr[(\sum_{i\in S}r_i)_j=1\ \forall j\in T]=(|S|/n)^{|T|}$. Hence for fixed $S$, $\sum_{i\in S}r_i$ has i.i.d. $\mathrm{Bern}(k/n)=\mathrm{Bern}(p)$ coordinates. Equal marginals alone do **not** give the distributional identity.
2. **Mixing over $S$.** Since the conditional law given $S$ is the *same* for every $S$ of size $k$, the unconditional law (averaging over uniform $S$ chosen independently of $M$) is unchanged.

Combine 1+2 to conclude $\sum_{i\in S}r_i\sim\mathrm{Bern}(p)^m$, hence $Y=\langle w,\sum_{i\in S}r_i\rangle\stackrel{d}{=}\langle w,v\rangle=X$.

comments.author: solver-agent
comments.body:
**Resolved.** The current `solution.tex` contains a fully rigorous proof of the distributional identity $Y\stackrel{d}{=}X$ that addresses both gaps raised in this issue. I verified the mathematics is correct (including a numerical check of the *joint* law below).

**How the two required points are handled (Claim `cl:dist`):**

The model is set up cleanly: column positions $C_1,\dots,C_m$ are i.i.d. uniform on $[n]$, with $M_{ij}=\mathbf 1[C_j=i]$, and $S$ is chosen independently of $(C_1,\dots,C_m)$.

*Step 1 (independence across columns).* The key observation is that, since each column has a single $1$,
$$u_j=\sum_{i\in S}(r_i)_j=\sum_{i\in S}\mathbf 1[C_j=i]=\mathbf 1[C_j\in S],$$
so $u_j$ is a measurable function of $C_j$ **alone**. Because $C_1,\dots,C_m$ are independent, $u_1,\dots,u_m$ are independent (functions of independent r.v.'s). With the marginal $\Pr[u_j=1\mid S]=|S|/n=k/n=p$, this yields the full conditional joint law
$$\Pr[u=b\mid S]=\prod_{j=1}^m p^{b_j}(1-p)^{1-b_j}\quad(b\in\{0,1\}^m),$$
i.e. conditionally on $S$, $u\sim\mathrm{Bern}(p)^m$. The proof explicitly flags this as the step the marginal-only sketch missed.

*Step 2 (mixing over $S$).* Since the conditional law `eq:condlaw` is the **same constant** for every $k$-set $S$, and $S\perp(C_1,\dots,C_m)$, total probability gives $\Pr[u=b]=\big(\sum_{|S|=k}\Pr[S]\big)\prod_j p^{b_j}(1-p)^{1-b_j}=\prod_j p^{b_j}(1-p)^{1-b_j}=\Pr[v=b]$.

Hence $u\sim\mathrm{Bern}(p)^m=v$ and $Y=\langle w,u\rangle\stackrel{d}{=}\langle w,v\rangle=X$.

**Numerical verification.** I computed the exact joint law of $u=\sum_{i\in S}r_i$ (brute force over all $S$ and all $(C_1,\dots,C_m)$) and confirmed it equals $\mathrm{Bern}(p)^m$ to machine precision for $(n,m,k)=(4,3,2),(6,3,2),(5,2,2)$, i.e. $p=1/2,1/3,2/5$. The full joint distribution matched, not just marginals.
